# A collision in generated files is regenerated, not repaired

Both collisions in the run that closed #99–#103 and #113 included `skills/kntnt/catalog.json`, and every future wave that merges two Skill-touching tickets will collide there again, predictably and forever. That file is the output of a deterministic command over the tree, so two builders who each regenerated it honestly produce two different versions of a file neither of them decided anything about. ADR-0071 took the collisions that carry no disagreement out of the append-only files by making the run write them; a generated file cannot be appended to and stayed behind, costing a routed repair subagent and a full re-verification per collision to reproduce what one command already knows.

**A collision confined to files the repository declares generated is settled by running their generators on the merged tree and committing the result, and no repair is dispatched for it.** There is nothing in such a collision for a session to settle: the merged tree already determines what the file says, and running the generator there is what says it. What the repair path would buy is a subagent reading two ticket bodies to reach, at best, the bytes the command produces — and, at worst, a hand-merged version of a file no hand should write.

**What counts as generated is read off a declaration, never inferred.** The repository declares it in `.kntnt-orchestrate/generated.json`, beside the ticket notes the run already writes there, naming each generated output and the command that produces it; this repository declares the Catalog with the line its contributing guide already tells a contributor to run, and the suite holds the two spellings to each other. A recogniser would have decided the question for repositories that never answered it, and guessing wrong here means a builder's decision quietly overwritten by a command — which is the one failure this whole mechanism must not be capable of. A declaration that is absent, unreadable, or malformed declares nothing, and every failure of shape can only narrow the declared set, so the worst a broken declaration costs is the repair path the collision would have taken anyway.

**A collision touching any file no declaration names takes the repair path unchanged, and the mixed case is such a collision.** A collision that touched both a generated file and an authored one is a disagreement with a generated file beside it, and the disagreement is what decides where it goes. Settling the generated half first would hand the repair subagent a working tree already carrying a resolution nobody dispatched and no verdict covers, against a brief whose whole premise is that it settles what the merge could not.

**A generator that fails, or that leaves any file the merge could not settle, has settled nothing.** The merge is left standing exactly as it was, the ordinary refusal reads the collision off it and undoes it, and the run goes to the repair path with the answer it always had. A regeneration is therefore only ever an improvement on the outcome without it: it cannot leave the branch in a state nobody planned, because the branch is not touched until the merge commit itself.

**What licenses that commit ahead of a verdict is the reading that follows it.** The run already commits to the run branch without a verdict of its own — the wave's notes are applied there one ticket at a time (ADR-0071) — and what makes that honest is that the wave check reads the branch whole afterwards (ADR-0072), so the run's own writing passes the same verification as the work it describes. A regeneration sits inside exactly that arrangement: it is on the branch before any verdict, and no verdict after it can miss it.

This **narrows ADR-0055** in the one half where its account claims every collision. Everything that record settles about a collision two builders' decisions produced stands untouched: the repair on the losing ticket's own branch, the independent verdict on that resolution, the single rebuild where the verdict fails, and the reported pair naming the blocking edge the breakdown missed. What is narrowed is its reach — a collision carrying no decision is no longer one of its cases — and, for that class alone, its rule that nothing reaches the run branch before a verdict passes it.

**The road not taken was making the README run-owned as well.** It is the other file this repository's waves keep colliding in, and the run could own it exactly as it owns the changelog. It is rejected because several tickets name a README section in their own acceptance criteria: a builder that must ship one to pass independent verification is the ownership working, not failing, and a run-owned README would leave a verifier reading for a section its builder was forbidden to write. The record showed that repair to be cheap, which is what makes waiting for the collision the better trade. The distinction is not README against Catalog but decided against derived: a section somebody writes is a decision, and a decision is repaired.

**What this costs.** The engine now runs a command the repository declares, through a shell, in the run branch's working tree, on a conflicted merge — the shell because that is how a guide writes such a line, with an environment assignment in front of it and a redirection in it, and a declaration a contributor cannot copy from the guide beside it is one that will drift from it. That is execution on the strength of a repository file, which is the trust the merge itself already extends to the same tree, and it is stated here rather than discovered. The declaration names exact paths rather than patterns, so a repository whose generated output is a directory lists it file by file, and a new generated file that nobody adds to the declaration collides as it did before — silently taking the repair path rather than failing, which is the safe direction but not a loud one. A generator that writes outside what it declares settles nothing, the run committing no tree its declaration does not account for; what it wrote there is left standing rather than reverted by a run that did not write it, so that failure is met as a working tree a developer has to look at rather than as a commit nobody meant. And a generator whose output is not purely a function of the tree — a timestamp, a network fetch, a machine-dependent ordering — produces bytes no second run reproduces; nothing here can detect that, and the wave check reading the result is the only guard there is.
